steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a regret-based defense for deep RL agents against observation-perturbing adversaries. Motivate why existing defenses fall short and list our contributions (the regret measure, its approximation, and the different algorithms and experiments).

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. DRL success and vulnerability to input attacks
2. Limits of existing defenses (adversarial training, maximin, regularization)
3. Our idea: regret-based defense
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. DRL success and vulnerability
- DNNs in DRL -> outstanding results, complex and safety-critical tasks (self-driving)
- DNN performance vulnerable to input attacks -> affects DRL
- adversary alters only observations, not underlying state or dynamics (transition function)
- even limited perturbations -> harm to property, loss of life in high-risk tasks
- example: stop sign digitally + physically altered to attack object recognition model

2. Existing defenses
- adversarial training (supervised training against adversarial examples): mitigates known examples, no guarantee to generalize to unseen adversaries
- naive adversarial training in RL: unstable training, lowered performance, if effective at all
- need inherently robust algorithms, not tailored to specific perturbations
- goal: determine risky behavior/states and reduce them across horizon, rather than value-optimal for many known examples
- maximin: maximize minimum reward; robust but trades unperturbed solution quality for lower bound
- regularization: adversarial loss terms keep actions unchanged across similar inputs; lowers attack success probability; still vulnerable when attacks succeed (shown empirically later)

3. Our approach
- regret-based adversarial defense: reduce impact of a successful attack, not overly conservative

4. Contributions
- formal definition of regret with observation-perturbing adversary: value without vs. with adversary
- approximation: Cumulative Contradictory Expected Regret (CCER), optimal sub-structure -> scalable; value iteration approach RAD-DRN (Regret-based Adversarial Defense with Deep Regret Networks); balances robustness and nominal quality
- policy gradient approach RAD-PPO: derive gradient w.r.t. regret, use in PPO
- RAD-CHT: Cognitive Hierarchy Theory, generates potential adversarial policies, regret-based robust response; CCER in adversary-reactive frameworks
- experiments: MuJoCo, Atari, Highway; vs. leading adversarial RL approaches; strong greedy attacks (e.g., PGD); also multi-step attack strategies computed directly against victim policy

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Using Deep Neural Networks in DRL lets RL models get outstanding results on complex tasks, and even on safety-critical tasks like self-driving. But DNN performance is known to be vulnerable to attacks on the input, and this also affects the DRL models that rely on them. In these perturbations the adversary only changes the observations that the RL agent receives, and does not change the underlying state or the dynamics (transition function) of the environment. Even when the perturbations are limited, high-risk tasks like self-driving give opportunities for significant harm to property and loss of life. One example of this is from prior work where a stop sign is altered both digitally and physically to attack an object recognition model.

Adversarial training (supervised training against adversarial examples) can mitigate how effective the known adversarial examples are, but it does not guarantee that the model can generalize to adversaries it has not seen. Also, it has been shown that naive adversarial training in RL leads to unstable training and lower agent performance, if it is effective at all. So we need algorithms that are inherently robust and not tailored to specific adversarial perturbations. Instead of developing a policy that is value-optimal for as many known examples as possible, we want to figure out which behavior and states involve risk and reduce them across the horizon.

- maximin: maximize minimum reward; robust but trades unperturbed solution quality for lower bound
- regularization: adversarial loss terms keep actions unchanged across similar inputs; lower attack success probability; still vulnerable when attacks succeed (shown empirically later)

Our approach
- regret-based adversarial defense: reduce impact of a successful attack, not overly conservative

Contributions
- formal definition of regret with observation-perturbing adversary: value without vs. with adversary
- CCER (Cumulative Contradictory Expected Regret), optimal sub-structure -> scalable; value iteration approach RAD-DRN (Regret-based Adversarial Defense with Deep Regret Networks); balances robustness and nominal quality
- RAD-PPO: policy gradient w.r.t. regret, used in PPO
- RAD-CHT: Cognitive Hierarchy Theory, generates potential adversarial policies, regret-based robust response
- experiments: MuJoCo, Atari, Highway; strong greedy attacks (e.g., PGD); multi-step attacks computed against victim policy

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Using Deep Neural Networks in DRL lets RL models get outstanding results on complex tasks, and even on safety-critical tasks like self-driving. But DNN performance is known to be vulnerable to attacks on the input, and this also affects the DRL models that rely on them. In these perturbations the adversary only changes the observations that the RL agent receives, and does not change the underlying state or the dynamics (transition function) of the environment. Even when the perturbations are limited, high-risk tasks like self-driving give opportunities for significant harm to property and loss of life. One example of this is from prior work where a stop sign is altered both digitally and physically to attack an object recognition model.

Adversarial training (supervised training against adversarial examples) can mitigate how effective the known adversarial examples are, but it does not guarantee that the model can generalize to adversaries it has not seen. Also, it has been shown that naive adversarial training in RL leads to unstable training and lower agent performance, if it is effective at all. So we need algorithms that are inherently robust and not tailored to specific adversarial perturbations. Instead of developing a policy that is value-optimal for as many known examples as possible, we want to figure out which behavior and states involve risk and reduce them across the horizon.

Maximin methods try to do this by maximizing the minimum reward of a policy, which can be robust but often trades away unperturbed solution quality to improve the lower bound. Regularization methods build adversarial loss terms so that actions stay the same across similar inputs, which reduces the probability that an adversarial attack succeeds. But as we show empirically later, they are still vulnerable when attacks do succeed.

So we provide a regret-based adversarial defense approach which tries to reduce the impact of a successful attack without being too conservative.

Our contributions are:

- We formally define regret in settings where there is an observation-perturbing adversary. Basically, regret is the difference between the value achieved without and with an observation-perturbing adversary.

- We derive an approximation of regret called Cumulative Contradictory Expected Regret (CCER), which can be optimized in a scalable way because it satisfies the optimal sub-structure property. We give a value iteration approach to minimize CCER called RAD-DRN (Regret-based Adversarial Defense with Deep Regret Networks). With CCER our approach can balance robustness and nominal solution quality.

- We give a policy gradient approach to minimize CCER called RAD-PPO. We derive the policy gradient with respect to the regret measure and use it in the PPO framework.

- We give an approach based on Cognitive Hierarchy Theory called RAD-CHT that generates potential adversarial policies and computes a regret-based robust response, to show how CCER can be applied in adversary-reactive frameworks.

- Finally, we give detailed experimental results on multiple benchmark problems (MuJoCo, Atari, and Highway) to show the utility of our approaches against several leading approaches in adversarial RL. Like previous approaches, we show the performance of our approach against strong greedy attacks (e.g., PGD). Unlike existing work, we also show that it is effective against multi-step attack strategies that are computed directly against the victim policy.

steps.text:

In these perturbations the adversary only changes the observations that the RL agent receives, and does not change the underlying state or the dynamics (transition function) of the environment. Even when the perturbations are limited, high-risk tasks like self-driving give opportunities for significant harm to property and loss of life. One example of this is presented by [7], where a stop sign is altered both digitally and physically to attack an object recognition model.

Also, it has been shown that naive adversarial training in RL leads to unstable training and lower agent performance, if it is effective at all [10]. So we need algorithms that are inherently robust and not tailored to specific adversarial perturbations. Instead of developing a policy that is value-optimal for as many known examples as possible, we want to figure out which behavior and states involve risk and reduce them across the horizon.

Maximin methods try to do this by maximizing the minimum reward of a policy [11,12], which can be robust but often trades away unperturbed solution quality to improve the lower bound. Regularization methods build adversarial loss terms so that actions stay the same across similar inputs [13,10,12], which reduces the probability that an adversarial attack succeeds. But as we show empirically later, they are still vulnerable when attacks do succeed.

So we provide a regret-based adversarial defense approach which tries to reduce the impact of a successful attack without being too conservative.

Our contributions are:

- We formally define regret in settings where there is an observation-perturbing adversary. Basically, regret is the difference between the value achieved without and with an observation-perturbing adversary.

- Finally, we give detailed experimental results on multiple benchmark problems (MuJoCo, Atari, and Highway) to show the utility of our approaches against several leading approaches in adversarial RL. Like previous approaches, we show the performance of our approach against strong greedy attacks (e.g., PGD). steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Using the power of Deep Neural Networks in DRL [1] allows RL models to achieve outstanding results on complex and even safety-critical tasks, such as self-driving [2,3]. However, DNN performance is known to be vulnerable to attacks on input, which in turn impacts the DRL models that rely on them [4,5,6]. In such perturbations, adversaries only alter the observations received by an RL agent and not the underlying state or the dynamics (transition function) of the environment. Even with limited perturbations, high-risk tasks such as self-driving give opportunities for significant harm to property and loss of life. One such example is presented by [7], where a stop sign is both digitally and physically altered to attack an object recognition model.

Although adversarial training (supervised training against adversarial examples) can mitigate the effectiveness of known adversarial examples [4,8,6,9], it does not guarantee the ability to generalize to unseen adversaries. In addition, it has been shown that naive adversarial training in RL leads to unstable training and lower agent performance, if it is effective at all [10]. Thus, we need algorithms that are inherently robust rather than tailored to specific adversarial perturbations. Instead of developing a policy that is value-optimal for as many known examples as possible, we want to determine which behavior and states involve risk and reduce them across the horizon. To this end, maximin methods maximize the minimum reward of a policy [11,12], which can be robust but often trades unperturbed solution quality to improve the lower bound. Regularization methods construct adversarial loss terms so that actions remain unchanged across similar inputs [13,10,12], reducing the probability of a successful adversarial attack. However, as we show empirically later, they remain vulnerable when attacks are successful.

To address this, we provide a regret-based adversarial defense approach that aims to reduce the impact of a successful attack without being overly conservative.

Through our contributions, we:

- Formally define regret in settings where an observation-perturbing adversary is present. Broadly, regret is the difference of value achieved in the absence versus in the presence of an observation-perturbing adversary.

- Derive an approximation of regret, named Cumulative Contradictory Expected Regret (CCER), which is amenable to scalable optimization because it satisfies the optimal sub-structure property. We provide a value iteration approach to minimize CCER, named RAD-DRN (Regret-based Adversarial Defense with Deep Regret Networks). Using CCER, our approach can balance robustness and nominal solution quality.

- Provide a policy gradient approach to minimize CCER, named RAD-PPO. We derive the policy gradient w.r.t the regret measure and use it in the PPO framework.

- Provide an approach based on Cognitive Hierarchy Theory, named RAD-CHT, that generates potential adversarial policies and computes a regret-based robust response, to demonstrate an application of CCER in adversary-reactive frameworks.

- Finally, provide detailed experimental results on multiple benchmark problems (MuJoCo, Atari, and Highway) to demonstrate the utility of our approaches against several leading approaches in adversarial RL. Like previous approaches, we demonstrate the performance of our approach against strong greedy attacks (e.g., PGD). Unlike existing work, we also show effectiveness against multi-step attack strategies that are computed directly against the victim policy.
